identification.summary: Night Dragon is the name McAfee gave to a series of coordinated, covert intrusions against global oil, energy and petrochemical companies, described in a McAfee Foundstone/McAfee Labs white paper dated 10 February 2011 [S1]. Attackers used spear-phishing, social engineering, Windows vulnerabilities, Active Directory compromise and remote administration tools (RATs), and stole proprietary operations and project-financing information such as oil and gas field bid data [S1][S2]. McAfee's Dmitri Alperovitch said no zero-day exploits were used [S2]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks it as campaign C0002, with an older group object G0014 [S5].
identification.firstObserved: McAfee: activity began in November 2009 [S1][S2]. The ICS-CERT advisory says activity began in 2009 or possibly as early as 2007 [S3].
identification.notes: Night Dragon is a McAfee campaign name, not a Microsoft-named actor; no Microsoft name or mapping was found in the sources gathered. Treat it as a campaign label for one intrusion set in 2009-2011, not a continuing group. Third-party mirrors of ATT&CK data mention an alias 'Musical Chairs' but I could not verify it on a primary page, so it is not added as an alias.

attribution.confidence: McAfee said the tools and network activity pointed primarily to China, and described the evidence as circumstantial [S1][S2]. Some other researchers said they had detected the attacks but were less certain of McAfee's conclusions [S2]. McAfee traced C2 infrastructure to a person or hosting provider in Heze City, Shandong Province, China (sources differ on which) [S4]. Control Engineering reported that no one could say whether the Chinese government sanctioned the attacks or whether a private company was responsible (as reported in search results, not opened).
attribution.basis: McAfee cited Chinese-based tooling and network activity, and C2 infrastructure linked to Heze City, Shandong Province [S1][S4]. No government attribution to a named PRC organization was found in the sources gathered.

objectives: Theft of sensitive proprietary operations and project-financing information, including financial documents on oil and gas field exploration and bid negotiations and operational details on oil and gas field production supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems [S1][S2].

regions: Companies, individuals and executives in Kazakhstan, Taiwan, Greece and the United States [S2]
McAfee said it saw evidence of the activity in virtually every region of the globe [S1]
targeting.notes: McAfee confirmed five victim companies, none named publicly [S2]. NERC rated risk to bulk power system reliability as MEDIUM, noting financial data appeared to be the primary target although successful exploits may reach industrial control and SCADA systems [S6]. ICS-CERT said the tools and techniques can be highly successful against any industry [S3].

capabilities.summary: Unsophisticated but effective: spear-phishing, social engineering, exploitation of Windows vulnerabilities, Active Directory compromise and commodity remote administration tools, with no zero-days [S1][S2]. McAfee's paper documents the zwShell RAT and its command-and-control (C2) infrastructure in an appendix [S1]. ATT&CK lists hosted C2 infrastructure, HTTP-based C2 and password cracking with Cain & Abel, and a third-party mirror lists gsecdump, PsExec and ASPXSpy [S5].

campaigns.name: Start of Night Dragon intrusions
campaigns.summary: McAfee dates the start of the coordinated attacks on global oil, energy and petrochemical companies to November 2009; ICS-CERT says 2009 or possibly 2007.

campaigns.name: McAfee publishes Night Dragon report
campaigns.summary: McAfee Foundstone and McAfee Labs publish 'Global Energy Cyberattacks: Night Dragon'; McAfee confirms five victim companies and points to China-based actors on circumstantial evidence.

campaigns.name: ICS-CERT advisory ICSA-11-041-01A
campaigns.summary: ICS-CERT issues an advisory referencing the McAfee report, noting the energy-sector focus and that the techniques can succeed against any industry.

campaigns.name: NERC industry alert
campaigns.summary: NERC issues an informational alert on Night Dragon rating risk to bulk power system reliability as MEDIUM.

diamond.adversary: China-based operators per McAfee's circumstantial assessment; no named organization or state sponsor established in the gathered sources [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing, Windows vulnerability exploitation, Active Directory compromise, RATs including zwShell; no zero-days [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: zwShell C2 infrastructure supplied by one individual or hosting provider reportedly located in Heze City, Shandong, China [S1][S4].
diamond.victim: Oil, energy and petrochemical companies and their executives in Kazakhstan, Taiwan, Greece and the United States [S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection of bid, exploration and project-financing data suggests commercial and economic intelligence value; McAfee did not establish state tasking [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Windows and Active Directory enterprise networks, with exposure of SCADA-related operational data to intruders in corporate networks [S1][S2][S6].

gaps: I could not open the McAfee white paper, the ICS-CERT advisory, the NERC alert or the MITRE pages (fetch failed); statements are drawn from search-result summaries of these documents and should be verified against the originals.
Details such as the exact attack chain (for example web-server compromise and credential theft steps), full tool list and C2 indicators were not confirmed from opened sources.
Victim companies were never named publicly; the total number of victims beyond five confirmed is unknown.
No government attribution or Microsoft naming was found; sponsor is unresolved.
Whether Night Dragon activity continued after 2011 under another name is unknown.
The alias 'Musical Chairs' appears in third-party mirrors only and is unverified.
The Heze City/Shandong C2 link comes from McAfee-based press reporting; NERC text mentioning Shandong was not confirmed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Corporate networks of energy firms, Active Directory and bid or project-financing data stores are key terrain; SCADA data held on corporate systems is a secondary concern [S1][S2][S6]. STEP 2: Commodity tooling and no zero-days mean defenders' known-patch and credential hygiene gaps determine exposure [S2]. STEP 3: Template is spear-phishing or Windows exploitation, then Active Directory compromise, then RAT-based collection and exfiltration to leased C2 [S1]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued economic and commercial intelligence theft from energy and defense-energy suppliers. MDCOA is use of the same footholds to reach operational technology data in a crisis; NERC judged this lower risk in 2011 [S6]. Candidate indicators: unexpected RAT beacons from corporate hosts, anomalous Active Directory authentication, and bulk transfers of bid or financial documents [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track energy-sector compromise of installations that support DoD fuel and power supply chains [S1][S6]. (2) Authorities: coordinate responses through owners of commercial networks and sector channels such as ICS-CERT and NERC rather than assuming DoD authority [S3][S6]. (3) Mission assurance: separate corporate IT from SCADA and OT networks and verify what operational data sits on corporate systems [S2][S6]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DIB and energy sector partners; attribution was circumstantial, so prioritize containment over naming [S2].
